cues.text: A ball made of socks
Eusébio was born in 1942 in Mafalala, a very poor neighbourhood of Lourenço Marques, the city now called Maputo, in Mozambique.
He loved football, and he played barefoot with his friends on bumpy, home-made pitches.
They had no real ball, so they made one.
Roll up the sock ball.
The boys stuffed socks with newspaper and rolled them into a ball.
They called their team Os Brasileiros, after Brazil’s great team, and played using the names of their heroes.
You don’t need much to begin. Friends and a little imagination can turn almost nothing into something special.
The photo on the wall
Eusébio’s father, Laurindo, worked on the railway.
He had played football when he was young, and he loved the team Benfica.
In 1950, when Eusébio was eight years old, his father died of an illness called tetanus.
Lift the photo frame to remember him.
After that, his mother, Elisa, raised Eusébio almost all by herself.
There were five children in the family.
Years later, his mum and his big brother would help him make the biggest choice of his life.
When someone we love dies, it’s okay to feel sad. Keep their memory close, and lean on the people who love you.
Turned away
With some friends, Eusébio tried to join his favourite club, Desportivo.
They turned him away without even giving him a chance.
Another club, Ferroviário, said no too.
Eusébio later said the Desportivo coach was unfair to people because of the colour of their skin.
Open the third door.
At twelve, he tried Sporting Lourenço Marques, and they said yes to him and his friends.
He got his first real football kit, and from 1957 to 1960 he scored 77 goals in 42 games.
Hearing no is hard, and it isn’t always fair. Keep knocking, and stay close to the friends who stay close to you.
Far from home
On 15 December 1960, at eighteen, Eusébio arrived in Lisbon, in Portugal, far from his mum and from Mozambique.
Two big clubs argued over him, and the move took months.
For a while, he was sent to a quiet place by the sea, and he told his mum he was going back home.
Open the suitcase.
His brother had helped with the deal, and his mum signed it.
While he waited, he passed his school exam.
In May 1961 he played his first game for Benfica, and scored three goals.
Being new and far from home is hard. Stay in touch with your family, and ask for help when you need it.
The Game of Tears
At the 1966 World Cup in England, Portugal were losing 3–0 to North Korea.
Eusébio did not give up.
He scored four goals in a row, and Portugal won 5–3.
In the semi-final against England, Eusébio scored a penalty, but Portugal lost 2–1.
He walked off the pitch in tears, and players from both teams comforted him.
Bring in the hug.
In Portugal, that match is called the Game of Tears.
Eusébio still finished as the top scorer of the World Cup, with nine goals.
It’s okay to cry when something matters to you. Let others comfort you, and be kind when someone else is sad.
Clapping for the other side
In the 1968 European Cup final, Eusébio had a chance to win the game in the last seconds, but goalkeeper Alex Stepney saved his shot.
Right away, Eusébio stopped to clap for him.
Benfica lost 4–1 in extra time, but Eusébio still congratulated Stepney.
Clap for the goalkeeper.
The barefoot boy from Mafalala has been called Africa’s first great footballer.
In 2019, when Pope Francis visited Mozambique, he named Eusébio as an example of perseverance.
Win or lose, you can always be kind. Keep going, and be proud of where you come from.
